meta.title: The golden angle packs a disc
meta.description: Layout computed from the point's own INDEX rather than drawn from a noise or a scatter: point i sits at angle `i * a` and radius `c * sqrt(i)`, which is the arrangement a sunflower head, a pinecone and a succulent all use. The sqrt is what makes it a packing rather than a spiral — equal area per point, so the density is the same at the rim as at the centre — and the ANGLE is what makes it uniform. Both arms here run the identical expression and differ only in `a`. On the left `a` is the golden angle, 2.3999632, which is 2*pi times an irrational number: no point ever lands on a previous one's ray, so the florets interleave and the eye reads the two families of counter-rotating arcs nobody placed. On the right `a` is 2*pi/8, a RATIONAL turn, and every eighth point shares a ray: the same sqrt spacing collapses into eight spokes with wedges of nothing between them. That is the whole lesson — the packing comes from the angle being incommensurable with a full turn, not from the radius law, which both arms share. Distinct from the shipped `shape/spiral` primitive, which is Archimedean and evenly spaced in ANGLE: that draws one winding curve, this fills an area. Positions are overwritten wholesale, so the source only has to supply the right NUMBER of points and an index to read; a `pointLine` is the cheapest thing that does. Nothing here writes `scale` — a bare cloud draws every point the same size whatever `scale` says, and a column the renderer ignores would be a graph claiming something it does not show.
